faq.a: Switch for a single on/off that applies immediately. Checkbox for independent choices, possibly several at once.

mobile.features: Reach for a switch when flipping it takes effect straight away and there is no save step: notifications on, dark mode, auto-play. It is a pressable with `checked`/`onCheckedChange`, and the state is visible in the control itself, so it needs a label beside it that says WHAT is on. Note there is no `label` prop here at all — unlike `Checkbox`, which offers one and warns about omitting it. Naming the switch is entirely yours, usually with a `Label` or text beside it. If the change only applies after tapping a separate save button, that is a checkbox, not a switch.

do: Use for settings that take effect the moment they flip — the switch IS the commit.
Keep one switch per row with its label beside it, so the announcement names what flips.
Drive `checked` from state when the setting can change from elsewhere (server push, reset-all).
dont: Don't use a switch for form options that submit together — those are checkboxes.
Don't hide the state in color alone — the thumb's side and the track fill carry it together.

faq.a: Immediate effect means switch; submit-together options mean checkbox. If flipping it does nothing until save, it is not a switch.

faq.q: How does this differ from the web switch?
faq.a: Same `checked` vocabulary, same 52×32 geometry. The track and thumb are kern-drawn styles (with `switch-track-shape` theming the container) rather than Base UI parts, and state is `accessibilityState`, not ARIA.

web.features: Reach for a table when the data is genuinely tabular - several attributes per record, and the point is comparing them across rows. Give every column a header and keep the values in a column aligned, because the comparison is the whole reason the table exists. On a narrow screen a table that scrolls sideways is better than one that reflows into unrelated cards; a card list loses the comparison that made the table worth building. If each record stands alone and nothing is compared, that is a list, not a table.

do: Use tonal head rows over data rows for scan order.
Let wide tables scroll horizontally inside their wrapper.
dont: Don't center data text - start-align for scanning.

faq.a: Tables for multi-column data; lists for single-column rows with actions.

anatomy.name: TableRoot
anatomy.role: The `<table>` itself. The namespace `Table` also exposes all of the parts below.

anatomy.name: TableHead
anatomy.role: The `<thead>`. The header ROWS go here - see the warning below.

anatomy.name: TableHeader
anatomy.role: One `<th>`. A header CELL, not the header section. The names are one letter apart and they are not interchangeable.

anatomy.name: TableBody
anatomy.role: The `<tbody>`.

anatomy.name: TableRow
anatomy.role: One `<tr>`.

anatomy.name: TableCell
anatomy.role: One `<td>`.

anatomy.name: TableCaption
anatomy.role: The `<caption>`. Names the table for assistive tech - the only place a table gets a title it can announce.

mobile.features: Reach for a table when the content is genuinely tabular — the same few fields repeated per record — and the reader is comparing down a column. Columns are named and rows are keyed records of strings, so the data is a declaration and the table does the layout. Keep it to what fits: a compact screen compares two or three columns well and ten badly, and a row that needs to wrap into a paragraph wants a `ListItem` or a card instead. The table is a grid of text, so it is right for numbers and statuses and wrong for anything that needs its own controls per cell.

web.features: Reach for tabs when the content is genuinely parallel — the same thing seen from several angles, like a conversation's messages, details and files. Give each tab a short noun label and keep the number small enough that no label is hidden behind a scroll. Tabs are not navigation: if the panels are really different places with their own URLs, use links and let people bookmark them. Keep a panel's content independent of the others, so switching back does not lose what someone typed.

do: Use primary tabs under the top app bar for main destinations.
Keep one tab active; every tab references its panel via aria-controls.
Label icon-only tabs for assistive tech.
dont: Don't mix primary and secondary tabs in one bar.
Don't use tabs for navigation away — tabs switch views, they never leave.
Don't use fewer than three tabs — use segmented buttons or plain text.

faq.a: Primary under the app bar for main destinations (3px indicator, primary active text). Secondary inside content for sub-sections (2px indicator, on-surface active text).

anatomy.name: TabsRoot

mobile.features: Reach for a tabs when the alternatives are peers — different views of one record, different facets of one list — and any of them could reasonably be first. Each tab is data with a `value`, a `label` and optional `content`, and the group reports the selected `value`. The content riding on the tab is the useful part: it means the tab and what it shows are declared together, so they cannot drift apart. If the steps have an order and someone must do them in sequence, that is a stepper, not tabs.

Keep labels to one or two words; a tab is a signpost, not a sentence.
Drive `value`/`onValueChange` when the tab must follow app state (deep links, wizards); leave uncontrolled otherwise.
dont: Don't use tabs for a binary choice — that is a segmented button or switch.
Don't change the tab count after mount — the set is the navigation, not content.

web.features: Reach for text when a line of copy should sit on the typescale rather than on whatever size the browser defaults to. The variant picks the style; the element picks the meaning — a title rendered as a paragraph is a heading to everyone who can see it and a paragraph to everyone who cannot. Choose `as` for the semantics and `variant` for the look, and do not let one stand in for the other. If the line is a heading, it is a heading element regardless of how large it is drawn.

mobile.features: Reach for this Text whenever you are drawing words on a kern surface and you want them to sit on the type scale rather than in it by hand. `variant` names a TYPE ROLE — body, label, title, headline — and the size, line height, tracking, weight and font face all resolve from the kern typography tokens, so text cannot drift off-scale. The colour defaults to the theme's on-surface ink and `style` comes last, so a deliberate override wins while an accidental one stays visible in review. Everything a React Native `Text` accepts it still accepts — it is a `Text`, not a wrapper around one.

web.features: Reach for a textarea when the answer is prose and its length is the point: a message, a description, a bug report. It matches the input's border and type so a form mixing both keeps one rhythm, and it starts tall enough to signal that more than a line is expected. Wrap it in a Field so its label, help text and error are wired to it — the same as an input. If the answer is one line, that is an input; if it is a choice, that is not text at all.

do: Use for multi-line free text — comments, descriptions, messages.
Set `rows` for the initial height; allow vertical resize via CSS.
Label every textarea like any field.
dont: Don't use for single-line values — that is an input.
Don't fix the height where content grows — let it resize or auto-grow.

faq.a: Two rows by default (`rows=2`); grow with content or allow vertical resize rather than fixing a tall box.

mobile.features: Reach for a textarea when the answer is a paragraph rather than a phrase: a comment, a description, a message. It is the same component as `Input` with `multiline` forced, and the `multiline` prop is deliberately removed from its type so it cannot be turned off — a textarea that can become single-line is just an input with a confusing name. Everything said about `Input` applies here: inside `Field.Root` it takes its label and error from context, and its error is announced through `accessibilityHint` because React Native has no invalid state.

web.features: Built on IconButton toggle form with M3 state layers, `48dp` minimum touch target, and destination-named accessible labels per M3 accessibility guidelines (“Switch to light” while dark, “Switch to dark” while light). Supports uncontrolled zero-config drop-in backed by useColorScheme or controlled host mode and onToggle.

deviations.spec: M3's component elevation table names no toggle row. It tabulates "menu" and "rich tooltip" at level 2 and "dialogs (modal)" at level 3, but no row describes a toggle resting elevation.
deviations.kern: The toggle rests at elevation level 0 — no shadow token; level 0 is shadow: none.
deviations.why: A borderless round action has no container to lift — a shadow would invent elevation M3 never assigned. The level-0 claim is registered in the elevation inventory so it is asserted rather than assumed.

mobile.features: Reach for a theme toggle when the host owns the color mode and needs one control to flip it. The accessible name always names the destination — “Switch to light” while dark, “Switch to dark” while light — so the action reads the same before and after the press. There is no pressed axis and none latches: the mode lives in the host, not in the control, and the toggle reports the request through `onToggle`. The touch target is `48dp` with a decorative glyph hidden from the tree.

web.features: Reach for a time picker when the answer is a time of day and precision matters: a scheduled send, an appointment, a reminder. The fields are explicit rather than a single text box, so nobody has to guess the expected format. The invariant that matters is that the state is always 24-hour, whatever the display format — `12h` adds an AM/PM field without changing what is stored, so switching the display never changes the value. If the answer is a duration rather than a time of day, this is not the tool.

mobile.features: Reach for a time picker when the answer is a time of day: a reminder, a booking slot, a schedule entry. Each field is its OWN traversal axis — the web contract is one tab stop per field, and the picker mirrors it with a roving model per field — so a keyboard user can reach the minutes without passing through the hours. Twelve-hour is PRESENTATION, never state: the value is 24-hour internally and always normalised before it is reported, so a consumer that persists it cannot drift. `step` sets minute granularity, and an out-of-range value can never reach `onValueChange`.

web.features: Reach for a toggle group when several related on-off or select-one choices belong in a single bar of controls: text alignment, visible columns, a date range's ends. The group is the segmented control — one container, one row of options, and the pressed one reads against the rest. Choose the mode deliberately: exclusive when the options are alternatives, multi-select when they are independent flags. If the options are alternatives but too many to fit in a bar, that is a radio group or a select.

deviations.spec: Material 3 defines no tonal surface role. Its surface roles are the surface, surface-dim, surface-bright and the surface-container family.
deviations.kern: The group's container is painted with `--sys-color-surface-tonal`, a role kern adds beyond M3's 45.
deviations.why: A segmented control needs a track that reads as a container rather than as content, and none of M3's surface-container roles is tuned for a pill-shaped track holding pressed states. The role is registered as K3 in the role inventory, so it is a declared addition to the legal role space rather than a colour invented in a stylesheet. It is the token that deviates; this is simply the component whose whole look depends on it.

anatomy.name: ToggleGroupRoot
anatomy.role: The track. Owns the selection model — exclusive or multi-select — and the aggregate value.

anatomy.name: ToggleGroupItem
anatomy.role: One option. Takes the same props as `Toggle`, because it is a `Toggle` in a group; its `value` is what it contributes to the selection.

anatomy.name: ToggleGroup
anatomy.role: The namespace object: Root and Item.

mobile.features: Reach for a toggle group when several toggles behave as one control: a toolbar of formatting switches, a set of filters. The group owns the selection and the options are data. The one thing to understand before you start is `value`: it is a `string` for an exclusive group and a `string[]` when `multiple` is set, and the type says `string | string[]` because the prop genuinely changes shape with that flag. That means your `onValueChange` handler has to handle both unless you know which mode you are in — and you should know, because it is one boolean away.

web.features: Reach for a toggle when the thing is a button first and a state second: bold in a toolbar, a pinned item, a starred row. It is pressed or it is not, and it looks like the button you pressed to get there. Inside a ToggleGroup it becomes one option in a set — pass it a `value` and it joins the group's selection. If the control applies a setting immediately and has no button identity, that is a switch; if it picks one of several, that is a segmented control or a radio group.

mobile.features: Reach for a toggle when a button should stay down: bold in a toolbar, a filter that stays on, a bookmark. It is a pressable with `children` required, and its state is named `pressed`/`onPressedChange` — which is worth knowing before you start, because `Switch`, `Checkbox` and `Select` all say `value`/`onValueChange` for the same idea. The naming matches the mental model: a toggle is a button that stays pressed, not a value that is set. Use `ToggleGroup` when several toggles behave as one.

web.features: Reach for a toolbar when a set of controls belongs to a surface and should stay reachable while that surface is used: a text editor's formatting bar, a table's bulk actions, a canvas's tools. Group related controls and separate the groups, because a single unbroken row of icons is a memory test. Keep it to actions on what is below it — navigation and settings belong elsewhere. If the bar has only two or three controls, a row of buttons does the job and a toolbar adds nothing but a container.

do: Use as a floating action strip — formatting, editing, view controls.
Keep buttons to one concern each; separate groups with dividers.
dont: Don't use as primary navigation — that is a nav bar, rail, or tabs.

deviations.kern: The toolbar's bar is painted with `--sys-color-surface-tonal`, a role kern adds beyond M3's 45.
deviations.why: A toolbar needs a track that reads as a container for its controls rather than as content, and none of M3's surface-container roles is tuned for a rounded bar holding pressed states. The role is registered as K3 in the role inventory, so it is a declared addition rather than a colour invented in a stylesheet. anatomy.name: ToolbarRoot
anatomy.role: The bar. Holds the controls and moves focus between them.

anatomy.name: ToolbarGroup
anatomy.role: A run of related controls, so the bar reads as sections rather than a line of icons.

anatomy.name: ToolbarButton
anatomy.role: One control. A real button in the toolbar's focus order.

anatomy.name: ToolbarSeparator
anatomy.role: A divider between groups.

anatomy.name: Toolbar
anatomy.role: The namespace object: all of the parts above.

mobile.features: Reach for a toolbar when a surface has a set of actions that belong to it and should sit together: a document's formatting actions, an editor's commands. Actions are data — `label`, optional `onPress`, optional `disabled` — so the row is a declaration and every action is named by construction. That last part matters more than it looks: a toolbar is the classic place for icon-only buttons with no names, and because `label` is required here, that failure is not reachable. Keep the actions to what the surface actually needs; a toolbar that grows into a menu is asking for `Menubar`.

web.features: Reach for a tooltip to label an icon-only control, or to add one short line of context that is useful but not worth permanent space. It appears on hover and on keyboard focus, and it must be dismissible without precision pointing — if the content is only reachable by hovering, it is unreachable on touch. Never put an action inside a tooltip, and never put information there that is not available some other way. If the explanation is long enough to need paragraphs, it is a help panel, not a tooltip.

do: Name icon-only controls on hover and focus.
Keep text to a few words.
dont: Don't duplicate visible labels — tooltips name the unnamed.

faq.a: Visible labels win; tooltips cover icon-only and truncated cases.

deviations.spec: M3's component elevation table tabulates only the RICH tooltip at level 2; it names no plain tooltip.
deviations.kern: The (plain) tooltip popup rests at elevation level 2.
deviations.why: review-m3 ruled the plain-tooltip level a kern choice sharing the rich row's height, not a transcription of M3 (K11); the citation is the registry, not the spec row.

anatomy.name: TooltipProvider
anatomy.role: Shares open/close timing across a group of tooltips, so one does not fire while another is still fading. Wrap a group once.

anatomy.name: TooltipRoot
anatomy.role: Owns the open state for one tooltip. Accepts `open`/`onOpenChange` to control it.

anatomy.name: TooltipTrigger
anatomy.role: The control the tooltip describes. Hover and focus on it open the tooltip.

anatomy.name: TooltipContent
anatomy.role: The label itself. Portals to the end of the document and positions itself against the trigger.

mobile.features: Reach for a tooltip when a control needs one line of extra explanation: what an icon-only button does, what a setting means. The design decision worth understanding is how it treats the text. `label` is the TRIGGER's own accessible name and `hint` is the supplementary line — and the hint is carried as `accessibilityHint` whether or not the surface is showing. That is deliberate: on touch there is no hover, so a tooltip that only exists while open would hold information nobody can reach. The text is never trapped behind the trigger. `placement` is `top` or `bottom`, and Material 3's default is above.

do: Name icon-only controls: `label` is the accessible name, `hint` the supplementary text — two separate strings, on purpose.
Keep the hint to a few words; explanations with actions are the rich tooltip's job.
Let focus drive it — `open`/`onOpenChange` exist for the cases focus cannot cover, not as the default.
dont: Don't duplicate visible labels — tooltips name the unnamed.
Don't put crucial information only in a tooltip — it must exist some other way too.

tokens.value: surfaceContainer with 12/8/16dp padding and real buttons

faq.a: A label for an unnamed control means plain. A subhead plus supporting text plus actions means rich — and if the rich surface has no actions and no subhead, that is a plain tooltip.

faq.q: How does this differ from the web tooltip?
faq.a: Same trigger contract (focus opens) and same K11 level-2 resting elevation on the plain surface. The plain surface is inert (`pointerEvents="none"`, `role="text"`) so touches fall through to the trigger; the rich surface takes touches because its actions are interactive by spec.

deviations.kern: The (plain) tooltip popup rests at elevation level 2.

web.features: Reach for the top app bar when a screen needs a name and a place for its actions. It is Material 3's bar in three sizes, and the composition family around it is what makes it useful in a real shell: `AppTopBar` is the app-level variant with the menus already wired, and the four `*Menu` exports are thin wrappers over one `TopBarMenu` — apps, help, notifications, user. Grouping them here rather than giving each a page is deliberate: they share one implementation and differ only in which items they show. The sizes are Material 3's and they change the bar's HEIGHT, so the shell can lay out against a known number.

do: Name the screen in the title and keep the trailing slot to screen-level actions.
Use `AppTopBar` for the shell header — the standard menus are already placed and wired.
Reach for `TopBarMenu` directly when the menu is custom; wrap it only when the same items repeat.
dont: Don't invent a fourth size — the three Material 3 heights are the whole axis and the shell lays out against them.
Don't rewire the `*Menu` wrappers per screen — if the items differ, that is a `TopBarMenu` with its own data.

faq.a: `AppTopBar` is the shell header with the standard menus placed — reach for it first. `TopAppBar` is the bare bar for screens that need their own composition.
Small is the default screen header; medium carries a two-line title for top-level screens. The sizes change the bar's height, so the shell can lay out against a known number.

anatomy.name: TopAppBar
anatomy.role: The bar. Three sizes, leading slot, title, trailing actions — the screen's header.

anatomy.name: TopAppBarToggle
anatomy.role: The sidebar control. Reads `useSidebar()` itself, so the bar and the sidebar stay in sync with no props.

anatomy.name: AppTopBar
anatomy.role: The app-level bar with the standard menus already placed — the shell's header, not a blank bar.

anatomy.name: TopBarMenu
anatomy.role: One menu from `TopBarMenuItem[]`. The four `*Menu` exports are thin wrappers over this.

mobile.features: Reach for a top app bar on a native screen that has a title and one or two screen-level actions. It is the screen's header: where you are, and the things you can do from here. The size axis is the point — a small bar for most screens, a medium one when the title should carry weight. Keep the leading slot to one thing, usually back or menu, and the trailing slot to the actions that genuinely belong to the screen rather than to the app. If the screen has no actions and no need to say where you are, the bar is taking space for nothing.

do: Give every screen that has actions a bar that names it — the title is the screen's identity.
Pick the size by title weight: small for most screens, medium when the title should carry the screen.
Keep the leading slot to one thing (back or menu) and the trailing slot to screen-level actions.
dont: Don't put app-level navigation in the trailing slot — that belongs to the drawer or rail, not the bar.
Don't render a bar on a screen with no title and no actions — it takes space for nothing.

48dp touch target with a required label

faq.q: How does this differ from the web top app bar?
faq.a: Same family, different member: the web bar is the shell composition with menus (`@xoroh/kern/start`), this one is the compact bar with leading/trailing slots. Both name the screen and hold its actions — switch tabs, not patterns.

anatomy.name: TopAppBar
anatomy.role: The bar. Holds the title and the two slots, and fixes the screen's header height per size.

anatomy.name: TopAppBarAction
anatomy.role: An icon action sized to Material 3's minimum touch target. Its `label` is required — it is the action's name, not optional decoration.

anatomy.name: TopAppBarToggle
anatomy.role: The leading button that opens and closes the shell's rail or drawer. Its accessible name says what the press does (`Open navigation` while closed), and `expanded` carries the open state.

web.features: Reach for TopBar when a site needs its main destinations at the top of every page. You provide the brand, route list, current path, and optional actions; a `LinkProvider` lets the host router render internal links without making routing a package dependency. On narrow screens the links move into an accessible disclosure, and Escape closes it and returns focus to its trigger.

do: Pass the current pathname so the active destination and `aria-current` stay synchronized with the host router.
Keep the primary route list short enough to fit the desktop bar; put secondary destinations in a separate surface.
dont: Don't put action buttons inside `items`; use the `actions` slot for actions and controls.
Don't render two TopBars on one page; each adds a primary navigation landmark and sticky layer.

mobile.features: Reach for an aspect ratio box when something must not jump as it loads or resize: an image, a video, a map, a thumbnail. The `ratio` is width divided by height — `16/9` for widescreen, `4/3` for the older frame, `1` for a square — so the number means what it says rather than being a named format you have to remember. The box reserves its space up front, which is what stops the layout shifting when the content arrives. That is the whole reason to reach for it rather than setting a height: the height is derived, so it stays right at every width.

Reach for a boot splash while the app is getting ready and there is nothing yet to show. It covers the boot and swaps to your content when `ready` turns true — one flag, no timing to manage. The design decision worth knowing is what it does NOT ship: kern has NO brand mark. `mark` is host-owned, so the logo is yours and the splash cannot quietly become someone else's brand. And rather than only a spinner, `milestones` shows named steps with `currentMilestone`, which turns an anonymous wait into a visible sequence.

Reach for a contrast toggle when the host owns the contrast level and needs one control to flip it. The accessible name always names the destination — “Use high contrast” while standard — so the action reads the same before and after the press. There is no pressed axis and none latches: the level lives in the host, not in the control, and the toggle reports the request through `onToggle`. The touch target is `48dp` with a decorative “Aa” glyph hidden from the tree.

deviations.spec: M3's component elevation table names no toggle row. It tabulates "menu" and "rich tooltip" at level 2 and "dialogs (modal)" at level 3, but no row describes a toggle resting elevation.
deviations.kern: The toggle rests at elevation level 0 — no shadow token; level 0 is shadow: none.
deviations.why: A borderless round action has no container to lift — a shadow would invent elevation M3 never assigned. The level-0 claim is registered in the elevation inventory so it is asserted rather than assumed.

mobile.features: Reach for an error boundary around a screen or a route, so a crash in one place leaves the rest of the app standing. It is the native analogue of the web `ErrorBoundary` and works the same way: children render normally, and if they throw, the boundary catches and renders your fallback instead. The fallback receives both the error and a `reset` callback, so recovery is yours to design — and the source is explicit that recovery differs per route, which is why the fallback is app-specific rather than a default kern screen. Keep it high enough to matter and low enough to be specific.

Reach for an icon button target wherever an icon button sits in a toolbar or a tight row and needs its full touch area. It exists for one reason and the source states it: the platform minimum touch target is larger than the icon button's own box, so a toolbar needs this to guarantee the rest of the target. That gap is exactly the kind of failure nobody notices until they try to tap it — the button looks right, and the part of it that responds is smaller than the part that looks tappable. Wrapping is cheap and the alternative is a control that misses one tap in several.

Reach for this when you are building a pressable that is not a Button and not an IconButton — a list row, a card, a chip-shaped target, a custom control — and you want kern's accessibility defaults applied without adopting a visual component. It owns exactly three things and passes everything else straight to React Native's `Pressable`: Material's minimum touch target, `button` as a DEFAULT role rather than an override, and `disabled` reported even when the caller supplied only `selected`. Everything visual is yours. It is deliberately not a Button: it has no variant, no size and no styling of its own, because a wrapper that grew those would be a new primitive family wearing a thin name and would duplicate the decision `Button` already made.

Reach for list-detail when a collection and its record share one screen and the screen is a phone: mail, settings, a browse-and-read flow. It takes the SAME data shape as the web `ListDetail` — a list slot, a detail slot and one flag — so a shared app drives both renderers from one state; only the presentation differs, collapsing to one pane at a time. The back affordance is part of the component and only exists when a host handler provides it: a detail pane with no way back is a trap, so the pressable is wired to `onBack` rather than assumed.

Reach for a menu group list when you want the grouped-action list itself and intend to host it somewhere of your own. It is the shared piece underneath `MenuScreen` and `MenuSheet`, which is the point of the family: one data shape, two presentations, so a host can move an action from a screen into a sheet without rewriting it. Groups are declared as data — an optional heading and a list of actions — and a group with no heading is an ungrouped list rather than an error. Note that the heading colour is applied by the caller and not by the styling helper; the helper is public API whose `scheme` parameter is retained only for signature compatibility.

Reach for a milestone trio when a flow has a few named stages and the person should see where they are: onboarding, a checkout, a setup. The steps are labels and `progress` is the completed COUNT, so the display is derived rather than each step being styled by hand. The three states are the point: a done step is full, the current one is a pulsing loader, and what is left is dim. That gives the row a readable shape — you can see what is finished, what is happening now, and what is still ahead without reading a word.

Reach for a navigation bar item when you are building a vertical destination list of your own rather than using the horizontal bar or the drawer. It takes the same destination data that `NavigationBar` does, and only the container differs — which is what lets one declaration of your places serve a bottom bar, a drawer and a sidebar. It draws the same Material 3 active indicator, the pill behind the icon, when selected. The row has a fixed minimum height so a list of them reads as even rather than as rows that grew to fit their labels.

Reach for a navigation rail when the app's top-level destinations should stay visible while the body changes: a workspace, a tool with a fixed set of sections. It is ONE component with two modes, because the Expressive mapping says a persistent sidebar IS the expanded presentation of a rail — two components differing only in width would be a split without a difference. The destinations are the same `NavigationDestination` data the `NavigationBar` takes, so one destination list drives both surfaces. Collapsing is a VISUAL decision only: the label stays the accessible name in both modes, so an icon-only rail is never an unnamed rail.

Reach for a settings row when a setting needs a label, an explanation, and its control in one scannable line: a toggle with its name, a stepper with its unit, a chevron with its destination. The row itself is not pressable — activation belongs to the trailing control, so the row carries no accessibility role beyond its label. What the web blocks catalog composes from parts, native ships as one row.

do: Name the setting in `label` and explain it in `supporting` — one line each, truncated, never wrapped into paragraphs.
Own exactly one control in `trailing` — the row names, the control acts.
Keep rows uniform: same `56dp` height and `16dp` insets down the whole screen.
dont: Don't make the row itself pressable — the press belongs to the trailing control, and a pressable row with a pressable child is two targets wearing one label.
Don't stack two controls in `trailing` — split the row instead.

faq.a: A setting owned by a trailing control means settings row; navigation to another screen means list item. Control in the row, destination out of it.

mobile.features: Reach for shape art when an empty state, a boot screen or a hero wants a mark that is unmistakably kern without being a logo. It arranges `Shape` pieces in one of three layouts — `scatter`, `stack`, `arch` — and every piece is placed by FRACTION of the composition size rather than by pixels, so the arrangement holds together at any size. It is decoration through and through: no content, no meaning, no state. If something needs saying, say it in text beside it.

anatomy.name: ShapeArt
anatomy.role: The fixed composition. `layout` picks scatter, stack or arch; `size` and `opacity` scale and fade the whole mark.

anatomy.name: ExpressiveShape
anatomy.role: The single expressive mark. One classification-hued shape at a caller-chosen size.

mobile.features: Reach for a shape when you want one of the kern forms as a mark or a placeholder: a brand glyph, a loading shape, a decorative element. The radii come from the shape SCALE rather than being typed, so a shape is kern's shape and not a rounded square someone guessed at — and the diamond is a rotated rounded square, which is how it stays on the same scale as the rest. `color` is deliberately restricted to classification hues, so a shape can carry meaning but cannot be painted an arbitrary colour outside the system.

Reach for a sheet handle when the sheet can be dragged and the affordance should say so. It is a fixed pill at the Material 3 handle size on the reduced-emphasis variant colour — Material 3's handle, drawn as it is specified rather than approximated. The one rule that matters is the same one the rest of the family follows: only show the handle where dragging actually dismisses the sheet. A handle on a sheet that will not drag is a promise the interface does not keep, and every sheet in the family exposes a way to hide it for exactly that reason.

Reach for a snackbar when the result of an action needs confirming and nothing more: a message sent, a setting saved, an item removed. It appears over the content, it says one thing, and it goes away. The optional action is what makes it useful rather than decorative — undo, retry, view — but keep it to one, and keep the action reversible, because a snackbar that disappears is a poor place for a decision. One current API (ADR-020, no compat alias): queue toasts with `useSnackbar()` under a `SnackbarProvider`, paint them with `SnackbarViewport`. There is no single-shot `visible`/`message` component.

do: Confirm exactly one thing — sent, saved, removed — then get out of the way.
Offer at most one reversible action (undo, retry, view); the action fires `onAction` and dismisses in one press.
Wrap the screen (or the app) in one `SnackbarProvider`, render one `SnackbarViewport` where toasts paint, and call `useSnackbar().add()` from anywhere under the provider.
dont: Don't put decisions in a snackbar — a transient surface is a poor place for a choice; that is a dialog.
Don't stack snackbars without bound — pass `limit` to the viewport, or none of them reads.

faq.a: Low importance with an optional reversible action and auto-dismiss means snackbar; a required decision that blocks means dialog. Blocking never belongs in a transient.

faq.q: How long does a toast stay?
faq.a: `duration` per toast, default 4000ms; `0` or less disables auto-dismiss. `dismiss(id)` and `clear()` end them early.

deviations.spec: M3's component elevation table names no snackbar. It tabulates menus and tooltips at level 2 and dialogs at level 3, but no row describes a transient confirmation.
deviations.kern: The snackbar rests at elevation level 3 with the iOS shadow quartet — with the other interrupting overlays. Registered as K11 in the kern deviations registry — review-m3 ruled this resting elevation a kern choice, not a transcription of M3, so the citation is the registry rather than a spec row.
deviations.why: A confirmation has to clear the content it sits over. Level 3 places it with dialogs rather than one level below the web token; the old style value sat a full level lower, the defect the elevation-parity gate now guards.

mobile.features: Reach for this when a pressable needs pressed feedback and whole-control opacity would dim the label too — Material 3 never dims a control to signal press. The wash reads its opacity from the DTCG states token, so a token change moves every control at once. It is paint, not content: pointer-transparent and hidden from assistive tech. The host Pressable keeps overflow hidden plus the matching radius, or the wash escapes the container shape.

Reach for a status bar when a screen needs a persistent status strip outside the content region: sync state, connection, draft count. The centered child is the status text; leading and trailing are slots for indicators or actions. It announces as a summary landmark, so a screen reader can find the status without entering the content. What the web blocks catalog composes from parts, native ships as one strip.

do: Keep the centered child to one short status — the strip is `32dp` tall and truncates to one line.
Put indicators in `leading` and actions in `trailing`; the middle belongs to the status.
Name it with `accessibilityLabel` where "Status" would not say which status.
dont: Don't load navigation into the strip — leading and trailing are indicators and actions, not destinations.
Don't duplicate the status in the content region — one status, one place.

faq.a: A persistent strip outside the content means status bar; a report inside the screen means banner. Chrome versus content.

mobile.features: Reach for a success transform when finishing should look like finishing: a form submitted, a payment taken, a step done. It has exactly two states and that is the design — `loading` and `success` — so the moment of completion is one component rather than a loader swapped for a tick by hand. The tick is drawn with the border trick rather than an icon, and the radii come from the shape scale, so it belongs to the same family as `Shape` and the loading indicators around it. The two colours are separate props (`color` and `successColor`), so the wait and the outcome can be told apart.

Reach for a supporting pane when the main content has a companion that is useful but not essential: an inspector, a preview, a summary. `supporting` is the companion and `children` is the main content. The behaviour worth knowing is the compact rule: below `compactBreakpoint` the pane hides ENTIRELY rather than squeezing — Material 3's compact breakpoint is 600 — because a secondary panel that survives by stealing half a phone screen stops being secondary. `currentWidth` is supplied by the host, since the component cannot measure the window reliably on its own.
